zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Mixed bag early, Spencer sorts it out late: yellowfin on the chunk after we chased the break south
subhead: A scrambled shelf edge cost us two days before Spencer's south wall came together on bait and warm water pushing 79 degrees.
body_markdown:
Grade for the week: C-plus starting out, solid B by Thursday. That's the honest read. We had two days where the troll spread looked like it was fishing a parking lot, then Spencer's south corner turned into the kind of stop where you're re-rigging ballyhoo faster than the mate can pitch them.

Here's the why. That southerly blow that rolled through last week did exactly what we said it would — scrambled the surface layer and blurred the temp breaks for a good 48 hours. When we finally got back out past the 20-fathom line, the sharp edge we'd been running to north of Spencer was gone, mushy, no definition on the water color at all. But the warm tongue didn't disappear, it just slid — south and a little east, tucked in tighter around Spencer's southwest corner, working the 39-15/72-50 stretch instead of the usual push up toward Lindenkohl. We flagged that displacement before it happened, and that's exactly where the fish showed up once things settled.

Water out on the edge is running warm — mid-to-upper 70s on the surface, pushing 79 in spots — and that's a full-moon tide doing what full-moon tides do out here: ripping current across the break hard enough to stack bait against the wall. Yellowfin have been the backbone of the week. Best action came on the chunk, not the troll, once the sun got low — butterflied bunker on a 6/0 circle hook, no weight, just let it flutter down through the chum slick in 40 to 60 fathoms off Spencer's south edge. Fish in the 25 to 45 pound class, a few pushing 60. Morning troll bite was there but thinner than I'd like — naked ballyhoo behind Green Machines and small Ilanders, spreader bars out the back, still connecting but you had to cover more water to find the willing schools.

Mahi have been a bonus, not a target, riding under whatever weed lines we crossed running out — schoolies in the 3 to 8 pound range under floating grass mats between the 100-fathom curve and Spencer proper. If you see the birds working a line, slow down, pitch a bare hook with a chunk of butterfish, and don't be shy about circling back.

Lindenkohl has been the disappointment of the four this week — same warm water signature should be there given how close it sits to Spencer, but the bait just hasn't set up the same way. We ran it twice, marked good structure on the machine, couldn't buy a bite either time. That's the kind of thing that happens when the edge relocates the way it did — Lindenkohl's contour doesn't hold the eddy the same way Spencer's southwest wall does, and this week that mattered.

Poor Man's has been quietly solid for the guys not wanting the long run. Closer to the beach, shallower water, and it's been giving up a mixed bag — smaller yellowfin, a scattered mahi or two, and enough white marlin activity on the troll to keep the outriggers snapping. Mid-August is right on schedule for white marlin building up along this stretch, and Poor Man's has had two or three raises most trips, sometimes more when the current's really moving on the push tide. Naked ballyhoo, small blue-white Sea Witches, run the spread a little tighter than you would for tuna — 20 to 30 feet back on the short riggers — and keep someone on the pitch rod with a dink ballyhoo ready the second you get a bill up.

Norfolk is the long haul out of Ocean City, and this week it rewarded patience. Bigeye have been showing on the night chunk in the deep water off the canyon's edge — 300 to 400 fathoms, drifting bunker chunks down deep with a glow stick on the leader, working the midnight-to-4-a.m. window when the current's slack enough to hold bottom without a ton of weight. Not a numbers game down there, one or two quality fish a trip, but they're big — 100-plus pound class. Wahoo have been mixed in on the high-speed troll running the edge at first light, deep-diving Yo-Zuris and Braid Marauders at 12 to 15 knots, single fish here and there rather than a pattern, which tracks — wahoo down that way tend to be a bycatch story in August, not a target.

Looking ahead, the moon's going to ease off full over the next few days and that should settle the current back into something more normal rather than the exaggerated push we've been fighting. If that happens the way it usually does, I'd expect the Spencer break to firm back up and possibly work its way back north toward Lindenkohl, which would put both canyons back in play together instead of one carrying the other. Best case, the warm eddy holds its current position through the weekend and Spencer keeps producing on the chunk after dark. If it slides again the way it did last week, we'll follow it — that's the whole job running this stretch, staying loose enough to chase the water instead of the spot on the chart. Worth keeping an eye on any tropical activity building out in the Atlantic too; a longer-period swell rolling in behind a storm system would be the next thing to reshuffle this deck, and we'd rather see it coming than get caught flat.
